title: U.S. House · Tennessee's 7th District
area: Middle Tennessee, including parts of Nashville's suburbs and Clarksville, under the congressional map Tennessee redrew in May 2026.

context.text: Rep. Matt Van Epps (R) won a special election on December 2, 2025 to fill the seat vacated by Mark Green's resignation, and was sworn in December 4, 2025. Tennessee then redrew congressional district boundaries in May 2026, and Van Epps is running for a full term in the redrawn 7th District.
Van Epps was unopposed in the August 6, 2026 Republican primary. Darden Copeland won the Democratic primary with 32.7% of the vote in a five-candidate field.

candidates.name: Matt Van Epps
candidates.ballotNote: Unopposed in the August 6 Republican primary

summary.text: Matt Van Epps is a West Point graduate and Army aviator who served ten years on active duty, then worked in business and in Tennessee state government under Gov. Bill Lee, including as Commissioner of General Services. He won the 2025 special election to succeed Rep. Mark Green and took office December 4, 2025. His campaign website says he is running for a full term supporting President Trump's agenda, and he sits on the Homeland Security and Science, Space, and Technology committees.

background.text: Born March 29, 1983, according to Wikipedia, which reports he graduated from Mentor High School in Mentor, Ohio.

Graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point in 2005 with a bachelor's degree in political science and mechanical engineering, according to Ballotpedia; he later earned a Master of Public Administration from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Graduate of the United States Military Academy at West Point; served ten years on active duty as an Army aviator, deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan and flying AH-64D Apache and MH-47G Chinook missions with the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment as a pilot-in-command and air mission commander.
Continued service in the Tennessee Army National Guard, rising to Lieutenant Colonel.

After active duty, served as senior vice president of operations at Main Street Health, a start-up focused on value-based rural healthcare, and worked as a consultant; Ballotpedia also lists him as founder of the consulting firm Darkhorse Strategy, LLC.

In Gov. Bill Lee's administration, held roles including assistant commissioner at the Tennessee Department of Veterans Services, assistant director of procurement and contracts at the Department of Transportation, strategic planner with the COVID-19 Unified Command Group, and Deputy Chief Operating Officer in the Governor's Office; he also served on the Tennessee Higher Education Commission.

Was named Commissioner of the Tennessee Department of General Services effective October 1, 2024, overseeing statewide procurement, real estate, and facilities operations, and stepped down on June 10, 2025 to pursue a new venture.

Won the October 7, 2025 Republican primary for the vacant 7th District seat with 51.6% of the vote in an 11-candidate field, then defeated Democrat Aftyn Behn in the December 2, 2025 special election, 53.9% to 45.1%; sworn in December 4, 2025. Renominated unopposed in the August 6, 2026 primary.
Serves on the House Committee on Homeland Security (including its Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security) and the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.
Lives in Nashville with his wife and child, according to his official House biography.

record.text: Won the special election for Tennessee's 7th Congressional District on December 2, 2025, defeating Aftyn Behn (D) 53.9% to 45.1%, and was sworn into the 119th Congress on December 4, 2025.
Serves on the House Committee on Homeland Security (Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security) and the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.

candidates.researchNotes: His official site issue pages are topic indexes without stated positions, he did not answer the Nashville Banner questionnaire, and no interview statements on the priority issues were found; floor votes are added separately from official records.

candidates.name: Darden Copeland
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 6 Democratic primary with 32.7% of the vote in a five-candidate field
candidates.currentRole: Founder and CEO of a political consulting firm

summary.text: Darden Copeland is the founder and CEO of Calvert Street Group, a Nashville public affairs firm, and says he previously worked on Democratic campaigns across the country, including for Rep. Dick Gephardt. He has not previously held elected office; he finished second in the October 2025 special Democratic primary for this seat and won the August 6, 2026 Democratic primary. He says he is running to focus on the middle class, affordability, and an independent check on the White House.

background.text: Born in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. According to his Candidate Connection survey, he grew up in a working-class family in Virginia and attended the University of Richmond.

Says he was involved in campaign leadership for Democrats including Gephardt, Gore, Lieberman, Kerry, Edwards, Kaine, Warner, Beyer and Kennedy; in 2025 he described serving as a campaign manager and political strategist on congressional and presidential campaigns.

Says he started Calvert Street Group, a national public affairs firm headquartered in Nashville, about 17 years ago; describes the firm as helping clients through local approval processes for projects such as solar generation, affordable housing, rural hospitals and mass transit.
Says he previously worked for then-U.S. Rep. Dick Gephardt (D-MO), whom he cites as a role model of "honest midwest values."
background.quote: Dick Gephardt was a champion of the working and middle class with honest midwest values. I was honored to work for him.

background.text: Says he has never run for or been elected to political office other than as an Elder at his church; sits on the boards of Historic Nashville, Inc. and the Nashville Wine Auction.
Ran in the special Democratic primary for this seat on October 7, 2025 and placed second with 24.9% of the vote, behind Aftyn Behn.
Won the August 6, 2026 Democratic primary with 32.7% of the vote in a five-candidate field.
Describes himself as married with two children and an Elder at Woodmont Christian Church in Nashville.

priorities.text: Says he is not a career politician and wants to be a consensus builder who reaches across the aisle for working families and constituents.
priorities.quote: If we're going to change the tone in Washington we need to change who we send to Washington. I'm not a career politician.

priorities.text: Says he wants to stand up to Republicans who won't challenge President Trump: "We need a strong Democrat that isn't afraid to stand up to the party and people in power and force them to come to the table and negotiate."
priorities.quote: We need a strong Democrat that isn't afraid to stand up to the party and people in power and force them to come to the table and negotiate.

priorities.text: Says he is passionate about standing up for the middle class and working families.

positions.summary: In a Nashville Banner questionnaire he said to protect and expand Medicaid in Tennessee, strengthen Medicare and keep the ACA's enhanced subsidies in place.
positions.quote: We need to protect and expand Medicaid in Tennessee.

positions.summary: In a Nashville Banner questionnaire he supported restoring the top marginal income tax rate for the highest earners, closing the carried interest loophole and strengthening the corporate minimum tax.
positions.quote: Restoring the top marginal income tax rate for the highest earners.

positions.summary: In a Nashville Banner questionnaire he said waging war should require a congressional declaration, with the President able to use military power to stop immediate threats.
positions.quote: waging war should require a Congressional declaration

positions.summary: In a Nashville Banner questionnaire he said he does not support a federal abortion ban and that a woman's healthcare decisions should be left up to her.
positions.quote: I believe a woman’s healthcare decisions should be left up to her and her alone.

positions.summary: In a Nashville Banner questionnaire answer on easing cost-of-living increases he said tariffs and "wars of choice" don't help.
positions.quote: Tariffs and “wars of choice” don’t help.

candidates.researchNotes: His immigration answer criticized deportations to countries migrants have no ties to while supporting secure borders; it was not recorded as a position on enforcement expansion.

candidates.name: Andrew Koontz

summary.text: Andrew Koontz is an independent candidate on the November 3 general-election ballot for Tennessee's 7th District. Ballotpedia lists no biography or Candidate Connection survey response for him.

candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website, biography, or public statements found for Andrew Koontz beyond his name appearing on the ballot. The Nashville Banner's voter's guide lists him with an empty questionnaire; the Banner notes he chose not to respond.

candidates.name: Lowell Reynolds

summary.text: Lowell Reynolds is an independent candidate, music producer and audio engineer, and third-year law student. He says he has worked in the music industry for more than 20 years. His campaign materials emphasize constitutional separation of powers, independence from both major parties, and support for small businesses and working families.

background.text: Attended Brown County High School and, per Ballotpedia, earned an associate degree from Indiana University's Jacobs School of Music (2002) and a bachelor's degree from Indiana University East's School of Business and Economics (2019).
Worked more than 20 years in the music industry as a producer and audio engineer; says his work earned him a Grammy statuette.
Holds a bachelor's degree in business and is a third-year law student; describes himself as a husband and father.
Has not held elected office; appears on the November 3 ballot as an independent.

priorities.text: Says Congress must reclaim its constitutional role and reduce power ceded to the Executive Branch.
Says he is not beholden to either party and, in a closely divided House, an independent could wield significant influence.
Says he supports policies that reduce burdens on small businesses and help working families build stability.
Says he supports building a high-speed rail system connecting major cities, with Nashville as its home city.
priorities.quote: I am very much for high speed rails.

priorities.text: Says elder care needs to be addressed, citing treatment of relatives who needed nursing home care.
priorities.quote: we need to address elder law.

positions.summary: In the Nashville Banner questionnaire he said he supports greater taxes at the top of the income scale.
positions.quote: Greater tax at the top, lower taxes at the bottom.

positions.summary: In the Nashville Banner questionnaire he said tariffs should end.
positions.quote: we need to end the tariffs, as they are just a tax on Americans.

positions.summary: In the Nashville Banner questionnaire, asked whether a president needs congressional approval to wage war, he answered yes.
positions.quote: Yes, and so does the Constitution.

positions.summary: Asked in the Nashville Banner questionnaire whether immigration enforcement in the second Trump term has been too strict, not strict enough or appropriately strict, he answered too strict.
positions.quote: Too strict. We need immigrants to survive.

statements.context: In the Nashville Banner candidate questionnaire (July 2026), answering whether he supports a federal ban on abortion

statements.quote: Allow and provide for more multi-family dwellings in lower income areas.
statements.context: In the Nashville Banner candidate questionnaire (July 2026), on how he would address housing supply
In the Nashville Banner candidate questionnaire (July 2026), answering whether the federal government should spend more or less on health care benefits

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and statements come from his July 2026 Nashville Banner candidate questionnaire; his campaign site is a one-page biography without issue pages. Immigration, abortion and health-care answers are short; the abortion answer addresses a federal ban only.

researchNotes: Van Epps' house.gov issues pages listed only topic categories with no dated statements suitable for citation, so his positions section is left empty; his record reflects his special-election win and committee assignments. No campaign website or public statements were found for independent candidate Andrew Koontz. Biographies for Copeland and Reynolds rest on their own Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey answers and are attributed as self-described; no biographical information was found for Andrew Koontz.
